conflicts.claim: Under the Surveillance Accountability Act, the agency that wants a person's data would decide whether its own collection of that data requires a warrant.
conflicts.detail: Each agency would decide whether its own acquisition of data is a search under section 3119 and whether an exception applies. A judge would review a search only when the agency concluded that a warrant was needed and applied for one. The bill requires no report or audit of the cases in which the agency concluded that no warrant was needed.

conflicts.who: Each agency that conducts a search
conflicts.claim: Under the Surveillance Accountability Act, the agency conducting a search would decide whether an emergency or consent excuses that search from the warrant requirement.
conflicts.detail: Exigent circumstances and consent are two of the exceptions in section 3119(b). The agency that benefits from an exception would decide whether it applies, and the bill requires no review after the agency relies on one.

professional.conf_note: No conflicts involving named individuals have been researched for this bill, which is not law and assigns no duty to a named official.

plain.sponsor: Rep. Thomas Massie, with Rep. Lauren Boebert
plain.status: Introduced April 23, 2026. Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary

cls.function: A bill to add a warrant rule to federal criminal law and a right to sue federal officials
cls.banner: The Surveillance Accountability Act is a bill in Congress. It is not law. If passed, it would change laws we already have. The government would need a warrant, which is permission from a judge, before it searches people. It would also need one before it gets their data from companies. And people could sue federal officials who break their Fourth Amendment rights. That part of the Constitution protects people from unreasonable searches.
cls.checks: Every type of check was run on this surveillance bill. The bill changes laws that already exist. So the review looked first at how it fits with those laws. That means their definitions and the ways people can enforce them.

stated.t: To amend title 18, United States Code, to ensure that all searches that significantly impinge on the privacy or security of a person require a warrant based on probable cause, to provide a right of action for violations of Fourth Amendment rights, and for other purposes.

marketed.t: The Act imposes a universal warrant requirement for any government search that significantly intrudes on an individual's privacy or security and closes the third-party doctrine loophole.
It creates a private cause of action that allows individuals whose Fourth Amendment protections are violated by government employees to sue for damages.

It would require federal and local government agencies to obtain a warrant, ban federal agencies from purchasing commercially available location or movement data, and prohibit federal pressure on local law enforcement to share warrantlessly collected surveillance data.
"Time to make Big Brother get a warrant."
marketed.l: Rep. Boebert, quoted in Rep. Massie's release

ladder.mechanism: The bill would require a warrant, which is permission from a judge, before the government searches people. It would also require one before the government gets their data from companies. And it would let people sue federal officials.
ladder.outcome: The bill aims to protect Americans' personal data. The government could get that data only if a judge says yes.
ladder.aim: The bill's larger goal is to end mass surveillance by the government without warrants from judges. Mass surveillance means watching large numbers of people at once.

promises.p: Representative Thomas Massie put out a press release. It says the bill would require a warrant from a judge for every government search.
promises.why: The bill states its warrant rule in broad terms. But it never says which agencies count as "the government". It ties the meaning of "search" to a test that courts made. Several of its definitions cover only searches aimed at one "specific" person. And it does not say how it fits with older surveillance laws.

promises.p: Representative Lauren Boebert put out a press release. It says the bill would cover both federal and local agencies.
promises.why: The bill uses the words "the government" and "a government entity". An entity is a group or body. The bill does not say if states, cities and counties count. Its new right to sue covers only people acting under federal law.

promises.p: The sponsors say the bill would close a gap in the law. That gap lets the government get data people share with companies without a warrant.
promises.why: The bill does ban the government from getting data that companies hold without a warrant, which is permission from a judge. But it lets the government skip the warrant when someone gives consent. It never says whose consent counts. It skips the warrant for public information too. And its meaning of "search" uses the same court test that made the gap.

promises.p: Representative Lauren Boebert put out a press release. It says the bill would stop federal agencies from buying location data that companies sell.
promises.why: The bill bars the government from getting "access" to data held by data brokers without a warrant. Data brokers are companies that collect and sell personal data. This ban would cover buying from them. But the bill never mentions buying, selling or contractors. It does not require anything of the companies that sell the data.

promises.p: Representative Thomas Massie put out a press release. It says the bill would stop the government from tracking people without a warrant. That includes tracking with face scans or license plate readers.
promises.why: The bill's part on face scans and plate readers is not a direct ban. It only limits the bill's exceptions to the warrant rule. And its wording can be read more than one way.

promises.p: Representative Lauren Boebert put out a press release. It says the bill would stop federal agencies from pushing local police to share data. This is data gathered without a warrant.
promises.why: The bill as first filed says nothing about federal and local agencies sharing data. It also says nothing about rules that come with federal grant money.

promises.p: The sponsors' press releases say the bill would let people sue for money when the government breaks their rights.
promises.prov: New section 1979A of the Revised Statutes
promises.why: The new right to sue covers rights "secured by the Fourth Amendment", meaning rights that part of the Constitution protects. It does not cover the bill's own new warrant rule. The bill also does not say if sued officials can use a common defense. Courts allow that defense under the older civil rights law the bill copies.

questions.q: The surveillance bill has a long full title. It promises warrants for searches that "significantly impinge on the privacy or security of a person". Where do its rules use that phrase?
questions.a: The bill's actual rules never use that phrase. To "impinge" means to cut into. The rules define a search with a different test. They ask if a person had a "reasonable expectation of privacy", meaning a fair reason to expect privacy. A court comparing the title with the rules would follow the rules.

questions.q: The surveillance bill says "The government shall not access" people's data held by companies. Which governments does that mean?
questions.a: The bill does not say. Its new warrant rule would go into federal criminal law. Its new right to sue covers only people acting under federal law. One sponsor's press release says local agencies are covered. If the bill means to bind states, it would have to say so. It would also have to rely on a power the Constitution gives Congress.

questions.q: Who makes, holds, moves, sells and uses the personal data in the surveillance bill? At which step does the bill act?
questions.a: Apps, phone companies, banks and device makers collect the data. Data brokers, which are companies that trade in personal data, combine it and sell it. Agencies and their contractors buy it or demand it. The bill acts at only one step, when the government gets the data. It does not require anything of the companies that collect or sell it.

s.l: CDT issue brief: the data broker loophole

questions.q: Which government agencies have gotten people's data from companies without a warrant before? How did they defend it?
questions.a: In 2018 the Supreme Court required a warrant for phone location records held by cell phone companies. A warrant is permission from a judge. A Defense Intelligence Agency memo was made public in 2021. It said the agency bought location data from smartphones. The agency did not read the 2018 ruling to require a warrant for data it bought. A 2022 report went to the Director of National Intelligence, the head of the nation's spy agencies. It was once secret and is now public. It described spy agencies buying large amounts of data that companies sell.

s.l: Carpenter v. United States (2018)
DIA memo on buying location data
Declassified report on commercially available information

questions.q: Say the surveillance bill stops agencies from getting people's data directly without a warrant. What is their next easiest way to get it?
questions.a: The bill leaves other ways to get data without a warrant, which is permission from a judge. An agency could use an older law that needs less proof. It could argue the new warrant rule did not cancel that law. It could collect data on everyone at once. Two of the bill's definitions of a search cover only a "specific" person. It could search data it already holds. The bill covers "acquisition and analysis" together, meaning getting and studying. It could rely on someone's "consent", or permission. It could treat bought data as public. Or it could have a contractor or partner agency hold the data.

questions.q: Which current laws let agencies get people's data from companies with less proof than a warrant? How does the surveillance bill treat them?
questions.a: Several laws let agencies do this. One is the Stored Communications Act. It allows court orders and subpoenas, which are legal demands for records. Others are FBI demand letters called national security letters, and a federal law on foreign spying. Banks must also file required reports. The bill mentions none of these laws. It does not say it overrides other laws. Courts avoid reading a new law as quietly canceling an older one. They usually say a specific law controls over a general one.

s.l: Coverage placing the bill in the section 702 debate

questions.q: If an agency breaks the surveillance bill's new warrant rule, what happens to it under the bill?
questions.a: The new warrant rule has no penalty of its own. Evidence would not be kept out of court, because the bill has no rule requiring that. The new right to sue covers breaking the Fourth Amendment. That is the part of the Constitution that bans unreasonable searches. It may not include acts that only the new rule forbids. An official who is sued can be expected to claim immunity, meaning protection from paying damages. Officials claim it under the older civil rights law too.

s.l: Egbert v. Boule (2022), on the limits of court-created damages suits against federal officers

questions.q: The surveillance bill says "searches conducted with consent" need no warrant. Whose consent would count?
questions.a: The bill does not say. Consent means saying yes. One part says a company's consent cannot replace a warrant for data it holds about someone. Another part limits giving up the warrant right in a contract. But the consent exception itself has no limits.

questions.q: Who would gain and who would lose if the surveillance bill worked just as written?
questions.a: People whose data companies hold would gain a warrant rule. It would protect them from the government. The same data would still be collected and sold to private buyers. It could still leak or be stolen in data breaches. Investigators would lose tools they lawfully use today. That includes fraud, child exploitation and missing-person cases. Critics of the bill point to this trade-off.

s.l: Decrypt coverage noting the investigative trade-off

questions.q: Would anyone have to report on, check or count how agencies search people's data under the surveillance bill?
questions.a: The bill would not require anyone to do so. It has no reporting rule and no audit, which is a formal check. It gives no role to an inspector general, the official who reviews an agency from inside. So Congress and the public would have no regular way to learn if searches without warrants from judges had stopped.

questions.q: What are the fewest changes that would make the surveillance bill do what its sponsors promised?
questions.a: The bill would need to say which governments it covers. It would need to let people sue when officials break the new warrant rule. It would need to say how it fits with older surveillance laws. It would need to say whose consent counts. It would need to cover bulk collection, meaning data gathered on many people at once. It would need to cover data agencies already hold. And it would need to keep evidence gathered by breaking the rule out of court. Ending the sale of this data altogether would take a separate rule aimed at sellers.

findings.pat: Open term for the regulated actor
findings.title: The bill never says which governments must get a warrant. State and local police might not be covered.
findings.plain: The bill says "the government" may not get your data without a warrant, which is permission from a judge. It never says which governments it means. The words could reach every agency at every level. They could also be read to mean only federal law enforcement agencies.
findings.tech: The bill uses "the government" and "a government entity" without defining them. An entity is a group or body. The warrant rule would go into federal criminal law. The right to sue covers only people acting under federal law. Both point toward federal agencies only. But one sponsor's press release says local agencies are covered. If the bill covers states, it would go further than the Constitution as courts read it. It would then need a power in the Constitution to bind them. That would likely be challenged in court.
findings.use: A state or local agency could argue the bill's warrant rule does not apply to it. A federal agency could then get the same data from that state or local partner.

s.l: Rep. Boebert release: "federal and local government agencies"

am.label: Define "government" with an open list that names the hard cases
am.instr: Section 3119(d) of title 18, United States Code, as added by section 2(a), is amended by adding at the end the following: "(3) Government.--The term 'government' includes any department, agency, or instrumentality of the United States, including any element of the intelligence community and any component of the Armed Forces; any State or political subdivision of a State; and any officer, employee, contractor, or agent of any of those entities."

ops.after: does not involve the use of enhanced surveillance technology or systematic monitoring.
ops.w: (3) Government.--The term "government" includes any department, agency, or instrumentality of the United States, including any element of the intelligence community and any component of the Armed Forces; any State or political subdivision of a State; and any officer, employee, contractor, or agent of any of those entities.

am.cost: This change would define "government" with an open list. The list would name federal agencies, spy agencies, the military, states, local governments and contractors. Because the list stays open, other groups could still count. Naming states raises the question of how far Congress can bind state governments. The narrower option avoids that question.

am.label: Define "government" with a closed list
am.instr: Section 3119(d) of title 18, United States Code, as added by section 2(a), is amended by adding at the end the following: "(3) Government.--The term 'government' means any department, agency, or instrumentality of the United States, including any element of the intelligence community and any component of the Armed Forces, any officer, employee, contractor, or agent thereof, and any State or local entity to the extent it acts jointly with, at the request of, or using funds provided by any of the foregoing."

ops.after: does not involve the use of enhanced surveillance technology or systematic monitoring.
ops.w: (3) Government.--The term "government" means any department, agency, or instrumentality of the United States, including any element of the intelligence community and any component of the Armed Forces, any officer, employee, contractor, or agent thereof, and any State or local entity to the extent it acts jointly with, at the request of, or using funds provided by any of the foregoing.

am.cost: This change would define "government" as a fixed list. The list would name federal agencies, their workers and contractors, and state or local bodies working with them. A fixed list makes things clear. But any body not on it would likely be left out. States would be covered only when they act with or for a federal agency. They would also be covered when they use federal money.

inq.q: What "the government" means decides which agencies the surveillance bill covers. Which real agencies would be in, and which would be left out?

items.h: Florida's wildlife police ran license plate searches. They did this for the federal immigration agency.
items.d: Audit logs are records of each search. They show that Florida's wildlife police ran license plate searches for the federal immigration agency. That agency is Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Each search checked more than 5,000 camera networks. The federal agency had no contract with the camera company. If "the government" means only federal agencies, the bill's warrant rule would not cover those state searches.

s.l: 404 Media on Florida searches for ICE

items.h: Border Patrol agents have searched license plate data. Local police had gathered that data.
items.d: Researchers at the University of Washington looked at Border Patrol. They found it ran hundreds if not thousands of searches of plate data from local police. The searches used a setting that let agents look up plates across the whole country. California's attorney general, the state's top lawyer, wrote to 20 police departments. The letters were about federal access. The attorney general also sued one of the departments.

s.l: NPR on federal mining of local plate data

items.h: The surveillance bill does not say if military and spy agencies count as "the government".
items.d: The Defense Intelligence Agency is a military spy agency. It made the location data purchases that became public. The new warrant rule would go into the part of federal law on crimes and police. The bill does not say if military and spy agencies count as "the government".

s.l: DIA memo on buying location data

items.h: The surveillance bill's new right to sue covers fewer officials than its new warrant rule does.
items.d: The new right to sue covers only people acting under federal law. Say a state officer searches for a federal agency. That officer could be sued, if at all, only under the older civil rights law. That lawsuit would have to be for breaking the Constitution.

inq.open: No court has decided what "the government" means in this bill. Representative Boebert's press release says local agencies would be covered. But the bill's text does not say so.

two.dec: No agency is in charge of the surveillance bill, and only federal officials can be sued. So who first decides which agencies count as "the government"?

views.why: The sponsors would likely want local agencies named in the bill. One sponsor's press release says they are covered, but the bill's text does not say so.

s.l: Rep. Boebert release

findings.pat: Definition imports the doctrine the bill targets

a.q: significantly impinge on the privacy or security of a person

findings.title: The bill defines a "search" with the same court test that has let agencies get people's data without a warrant.
findings.plain: The bill says a search is an act that intrudes on a "reasonable expectation of privacy". That means a fair reason to expect privacy. Courts used that same phrase to decide people expect no privacy in data they share with companies. The bill's title uses yet another standard. It covers searches that "significantly impinge" on privacy, meaning cut into it. That phrase appears nowhere in the bill's actual rules.
findings.tech: Courts have held that people expect no privacy in facts they give a company. In 2018 the Supreme Court narrowed that rule for phone location records. The bill lists kinds of searches. It is unclear if they count on their own or must still pass the court test. The bill's separate ban on getting data from companies does not rely on this definition. Courts may look at a bill's title when its text is unclear. So the title's different phrase gives agencies another way to argue for a narrow reading.
findings.use: Say an agency is sued for getting someone's data from a company. It could argue that was not a "search" at all, so no warrant was needed. A warrant is permission from a judge. The agency could also point to the bill's title to argue that only serious intrusions count.

s.l: Carpenter v. United States (2018)

am.label: Make the listed kinds of search count on their own
am.instr: Section 3119(d)(1), as added by section 2(a), is amended by striking "means any government-initiated act that intrudes upon an individual's reasonable expectation of privacy, including the following:" and inserting "means any government-initiated act that intrudes upon an individual's reasonable expectation of privacy, and, without regard to whether such an expectation exists under any judicial doctrine, each of the following:".

ops.q: means any government-initiated act that intrudes upon an individual's reasonable expectation of privacy, including the following:
ops.w: means any government-initiated act that intrudes upon an individual's reasonable expectation of privacy, and, without regard to whether such an expectation exists under any judicial doctrine, each of the following:

am.cost: This change would make the listed kinds of search count even if no court finds a privacy expectation. The bill also has a broad list of personal data. Together, almost any government handling of personal facts would become a search. That would raise pressure for clear exceptions to the warrant rule.

a.ctx: directed at a specific person or entity, or the property
collects information on a specific individual or entity

findings.title: Two of the bill's three definitions of a search target one specific person. Mass data collection may fall outside them.
findings.plain: Two of the bill's three definitions of a search cover acts aimed at a "specific" person. That means one certain person. Collecting data on everyone at once is not aimed at anyone in particular.
findings.tech: The first definition covers acts "purposefully directed at a specific person or entity". An entity is a group or company. The second covers surveillance that "collects information on a specific individual or entity". Only the third, on personal data, lacks the word "specific". But it has its own limit. It covers "acquisition and analysis", meaning getting and studying data. The sponsors say the problem is bulk collection. That means gathering data on many people at once.
findings.use: An agency could describe a mass data program as not aimed at anyone. It could then argue that the bill's rule requiring a warrant, which is permission from a judge, does not apply.

am.label: Name bulk data collection as a search
am.instr: Section 3119(d)(1), as added by section 2(a), is amended by adding at the end the following: "(D) Bulk collection.--Any acquisition, retention, or querying of data described in subparagraph (C) that is not directed at a specific person, including acquisition in bulk or by subscription."

ops.w: (D) Bulk collection.--Any acquisition, retention, or querying of data described in subparagraph (C) that is not directed at a specific person, including acquisition in bulk or by subscription.

am.cost: This change would count collecting personal data in bulk, without aiming at one person, as a search. A warrant must describe exactly what is sought. So bulk collection would in practice be banned, not just limited. That would affect agencies that study large sets of data for reasons other than investigations.

findings.title: The bill lets the government skip a warrant for searches "with consent". It never says whose consent counts.
findings.plain: Searches done "with consent", meaning when someone says yes, would need no warrant. A warrant is permission from a judge. The bill does not say whose consent counts. It could be the person the data is about. Or it could be the company holding the data.
findings.tech: One part of the bill says a company's consent does not replace a warrant for data it holds. Another says a contract cannot give up the warrant right unless the user agrees in a "knowing, voluntary, and explicit" way. That means the user understands, chooses freely and says so clearly. But the bill's list of exceptions allows searches "with consent" with no limit. The bill does not say how these parts fit together.
findings.use: A click-through agreement is fine print people accept by clicking a button. If it is labeled knowing and voluntary, it could count as the person's consent. The government could then claim that consent covers every search that follows.

am.label: Require consent from the person whose data it is
am.instr: Section 3119(b)(5), as added by section 2(a), is amended to read as follows: "(5) Searches conducted with the knowing and voluntary consent of the individual whose person, property, or information is searched, given to the government for the specific search, which may not be supplied by a third party that holds the information or inferred from terms of service."

ops.q: (5) Searches conducted with consent.
ops.w: (5) Searches conducted with the knowing and voluntary consent of the individual whose person, property, or information is searched, given to the government for the specific search, which may not be supplied by a third party that holds the information or inferred from terms of service.

am.cost: This change would require consent from the person being searched, given for that search. Consent from a company or from fine print would not count. But companies sometimes have good reason to consent. One example is reporting a crime against the company using its own records. The bill might need a separate allowance for that.

findings.pat: Exception that can absorb the rule

a.q: voluntarily made available by a person or entity to a public audience

findings.title: The bill lets agencies use public information without a warrant. That holds even if someone else made it public.
findings.plain: Information "made available by a person or entity to a public audience" would need no warrant. That means anything someone has shared with the public. A warrant is permission from a judge. The bill does not require that the person the information is about be the one who made it public.
findings.tech: The public information exception covers anything shared "by a person or entity". That means anyone at all. Agencies have described data they bought as public or for sale. Another part of the bill limits this exception for data "exposed to public view or accessible to a third party". A third party is someone else, such as a company. But that limit applies only to data gathered in public places and a few similar settings.
findings.use: An agency could treat data offered for sale to any buyer as public. It could then get that data without a warrant, which is permission from a judge.

s.l: Declassified report on commercially available information

am.label: Count only information people chose to make public about themselves
am.instr: Section 3119(b)(3), as added by section 2(a), is amended by striking "voluntarily made available by a person or entity to a public audience" and inserting "voluntarily made available to the general public, without charge, by the individual to whom the information pertains".

ops.q: voluntarily made available by a person or entity to a public audience
ops.w: voluntarily made available to the general public, without charge, by the individual to whom the information pertains

am.cost: This change would count information as public only in one case. The person it is about must have chosen to share it with the public for free. Narrowed that far, the government might need a warrant to read a news article about someone. The bill's separate exception for news outlets and public records would then have to cover that. So that exception should be checked too.

a.q: with respect to data gathered by entering a public place

findings.title: The bill's rule on face scans and plate readers is one unclear sentence. It may cover less than sponsors say.
findings.plain: One sentence in the bill is meant to protect people from face scans and license plate tracking. It is long and has several conditions. It can be read to cover much less than the sponsors describe.
findings.tech: This part of the bill only limits how the warrant exceptions are read. It is not a direct ban. It covers people who did not agree to data collection. That means collection in public places, on public roads or in businesses open to the public. The phrase "with respect to", meaning about, could limit only the consent part or the whole protection. The bill also lists face and plate data only as examples. So it is unclear if other data is covered.
findings.use: An agency could argue that data gathered somewhere not listed falls outside the protection. One example is data from an online platform, such as a website or app.

am.label: Turn the face scan and plate reader limit into a direct ban
am.instr: Section 3119(c), as added by section 2(a), is amended by striking "The exceptions described in subsection (b) shall not be construed to permit the warrantless collection, retention, querying, or analysis of data exposed to public view or accessible to a third party if the person associated with the collected identifiers did not express informed and voluntary consent to such collection with respect to data gathered by entering a public place, operating a motor vehicle on a public roadway, or patronizing a private establishment open to the public, including--" and inserting "Notwithstanding subsection (b), the government may not, without a warrant, collect, retain, query, or analyze any of the following data about an individual who has not given informed and voluntary consent to the government, regardless of where or how the data was gathered:".

ops.q: The exceptions described in subsection (b) shall not be construed to permit the warrantless collection, retention, querying, or analysis of data exposed to public view or accessible to a third party if the person associated with the collected identifiers did not express informed and voluntary consent to such collection with respect to data gathered by entering a public place, operating a motor vehicle on a public roadway, or patronizing a private establishment open to the public, including--
ops.w: Notwithstanding subsection (b), the government may not, without a warrant, collect, retain, query, or analyze any of the following data about an individual who has not given informed and voluntary consent to the government, regardless of where or how the data was gathered:

am.cost: This change would plainly ban collecting face or plate data without a warrant, however it was gathered. A flat ban would reach everyday uses, such as checking a plate during a traffic stop. The bill's exception for checking ID covers driver's licenses and other papers but not plates. So that case would need its own rule.

findings.pat: Savings clause wider than the rule

a.q: searches incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters

findings.title: The bill says it does not limit police searches during "ordinary" encounters. It never says what makes one ordinary.
findings.plain: The bill says nothing in it limits police searches "incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". That means searches that come up when police meet people in the normal course of their work. But the bill does not say what makes a meeting with police ordinary.
findings.tech: This part keeps the power of police to hold, pat down and arrest people. It also keeps searches "incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". Courts already have a settled rule that allows searches during an arrest. The idea of searches during "ordinary encounters" is wider, and the bill never defines it. Officials could argue this part wins over the new warrant rule wherever the two meet.
findings.use: Say an officer searches someone's phone at a routine stop. The officer could say the search was part of an ordinary encounter.

am.label: Allow only searches of a person during a lawful arrest
am.instr: Section 3119(e)(3), as added by section 2(a), is amended by striking "searches incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters" and inserting "searches of the person incident to a lawful arrest, not including any search of the contents of an electronic device".

ops.q: searches incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters
ops.w: searches of the person incident to a lawful arrest, not including any search of the contents of an electronic device

am.cost: This change would allow only searches of a person during a lawful arrest. It would not allow searches of what is on a phone or other device. That is narrower than what police do today in some settings. Police groups would object.

findings.pat: Remedy does not reach the new rule

a.q: secured by the Fourth Amendment, shall be liable

findings.title: People could sue over breaking the Constitution's search protections. They could not sue over breaking the bill's own warrant rule.
findings.plain: The bill creates a new warrant rule in one place and a right to sue in another. A warrant is permission from a judge. The right to sue covers breaking the Fourth Amendment, the part of the Constitution that bans unreasonable searches. It does not cover breaking the new rule. Where the new rule goes further than the Constitution as courts read it, there may be nothing to sue over.
findings.tech: The right to sue covers losing rights "secured by the Fourth Amendment", meaning rights it protects. The new warrant rule is meant to require warrants where courts say the Constitution does not. Data held by companies is one example. Breaking the new rule without also breaking the Constitution would give no right to sue. The new rule has no penalty of its own either.
findings.use: An agency could admit it broke the new warrant rule and still get the lawsuit thrown out. That is because no right in the Constitution was broken.

s.l: Carpenter v. United States (2018), on the current reach of the Fourth Amendment for third-party records

am.label: Let people sue over breaking the new warrant rule
am.instr: Section 1979A(a) of the Revised Statutes, as added by section 3(a), is amended by striking "secured by the Fourth Amendment, shall be liable" and inserting "secured by the Fourth Amendment or by section 3119 of title 18, United States Code, shall be liable".

ops.q: secured by the Fourth Amendment, shall be liable
ops.w: secured by the Fourth Amendment or by section 3119 of title 18, United States Code, shall be liable

am.cost: This change would let people sue when officials break the bill's own warrant rule, not only the Constitution. Federal workers could then be made to pay themselves under a new, untested rule. That would likely bring pressure to add a defense for officials who acted in good faith, meaning honestly.

inq.q: Which government acts would break the surveillance bill's new warrant rule but not the Constitution as courts now read it?

items.h: Getting bank records with no warrant would break the surveillance bill's new rule. It would not break the Constitution.
items.d: In 1976 the Supreme Court held that customers have no Fourth Amendment protection for records a bank holds. The Fourth Amendment is the part of the Constitution that bans unreasonable searches. The Court's 2018 Carpenter ruling said it did not change that. So getting bank records without a warrant would break the new rule but not the Constitution. The new right to sue would not apply.

s.l: Carpenter v. United States (2018)

items.h: Getting records of phone calls and internet use with no warrant would break the surveillance bill's rule. It would not break the Constitution.
items.d: The same is true of phone numbers dialed and similar records. A 1979 Supreme Court ruling covers them. The 2018 Carpenter ruling did not change that older ruling.

s.l: Carpenter v. United States (2018)

items.h: The Supreme Court has not said if the Constitution guards data that the government buys from data sellers.
items.d: The Supreme Court has not ruled on data the government buys. At least one agency has taken the view that the 2018 ruling does not require a warrant for bought data.

s.l: DIA memo on buying location data

items.h: The Supreme Court has not said if face scans or plate readers in public places are searches under the Constitution.
items.d: The Supreme Court has not held that either one is a search. The bill tries to protect against both. But the new right to sue would not cover them.

inq.open: Lower courts disagree on some of these practices. When a court finds no search under the Constitution, the bill's right to sue would not apply.

findings.title: The bill lets agencies skip a warrant in emergencies. It never defines an emergency or requires a later check.
findings.plain: The bill lets agencies skip the warrant rule under "exigent circumstances", meaning emergencies. They would not need a warrant, which is permission from a judge. The bill does not say what counts as an emergency. It also does not require anyone to review the emergency claim afterward.
findings.tech: The bill does not define "exigent circumstances", which means emergencies. So courts would use their existing rules on emergencies, which is a reasonable choice. Other surveillance laws allow emergency access too. But those laws make a court approve it afterward within a set time.
findings.use: Agencies could start to use emergency access all the time if no one ever checks it.

findings.title: The bill does not say if sued officials can use a defense that often ends lawsuits early.
findings.plain: The new right to sue copies the wording of the main civil rights law. Under that law, courts let sued officials avoid paying damages unless the right was already clearly established. That means earlier court cases had already made the right clear. The bill does not say if that defense applies here.
findings.tech: The new right to sue copies the main civil rights law. Courts let officials sued under that law use a defense called qualified immunity. A court would likely use that defense here too unless the bill says otherwise. For new surveillance tools, rights are rarely "clearly established" yet. The Supreme Court has sharply limited lawsuits against federal officers that courts created themselves. That is why a right to sue written by Congress matters, and why its details matter too.
findings.use: Lawsuits for money could be thrown out early because of this defense. That could happen even when a violation really took place.

s.l: Egbert v. Boule (2022)

am.label: Block the defense and set a minimum payment
am.instr: Section 1979A, as added by section 3(a), is amended by redesignating subsection (d) as subsection (e) and inserting after subsection (c) the following: "(d) Defenses; Damages.--It shall not be a defense to an action under this section that the right was not clearly established at the time of the deprivation. A prevailing plaintiff shall recover the greater of actual damages or liquidated damages of $10,000 for each violation."

Removing this defense for federal workers is disputed. Police and national security agencies would oppose it. Another option is to make the United States pay instead of the official.

findings.title: The bill does not keep evidence out of court when it was gathered without a required warrant.
findings.plain: The bill does not say that evidence found without a required warrant must be kept out of court. A warrant is permission from a judge. Keeping evidence out is the usual check on unlawful searches. That check would be missing for anything the bill adds beyond the Constitution.
findings.tech: Keeping evidence out of court is a remedy for searches that break the Constitution. Sometimes only a law passed by Congress is broken. Then courts usually allow the evidence, unless that law says otherwise. The federal law on tapping phone calls is one law that does say otherwise.
findings.use: The government could break the new warrant rule and still use the data it gathered against people. That includes criminal cases and other legal matters.

am.label: Keep evidence gathered in violation of the warrant rule out of court
am.instr: Add at the end of the bill the following new section: "SEC. __. EXCLUSION OF EVIDENCE. No information obtained in violation of section 3119 of title 18, United States Code, and no evidence derived therefrom, may be received in evidence or otherwise used in any trial, hearing, or other proceeding in or before any court, grand jury, department, agency, or other authority of the United States, a State, or a political subdivision thereof."

ops.w:
SEC. __. EXCLUSION OF EVIDENCE.
No information obtained in violation of section 3119 of title 18, United States Code, and no evidence derived therefrom, may be received in evidence or otherwise used in any trial, hearing, or other proceeding in or before any court, grand jury, department, agency, or other authority of the United States, a State, or a political subdivision thereof.

am.cost: This change would bar using information gathered in violation of the warrant rule, or anything found through it, in court. That could end criminal cases because of unclear wording elsewhere in the bill. It makes every other wording problem in the bill more serious.

findings.pat: No statement of relationship to existing law
findings.title: The bill does not say if its warrant rule wins over older laws that let agencies get data without warrants.
findings.plain: A warrant is permission from a judge, given when there is probable cause. Probable cause means good reason to believe a crime occurred. Several laws already let agencies get data without such a warrant. Foreign intelligence law is one of them. The bill does not mention these laws or say that it wins if they conflict.
findings.tech: The bill does not say how its warrant rule relates to other laws. It changes none of the laws on stored messages, FBI demand letters, foreign spying or bank reporting. Courts avoid reading a new law as quietly canceling an old one. And a specific law usually controls over a general one. The bill says it does not "authorize surveillance that would otherwise be unlawful", meaning illegal spying. It says nothing about surveillance that is otherwise lawful. The Senate's guide for bill writers says to name each conflicting law. It says a general override is unlikely to work.
findings.use: An agency could keep using an older law written for a specific case. It could argue the general warrant rule left that law alone. For spy agencies, this is the most direct way around the bill.

am.label: Name the older laws the warrant rule overrides
am.instr: Add at the end of the bill the following new section: "SEC. __. RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER LAW. Section 3119 of title 18, United States Code, shall apply to any search of, or access to data pertaining to, a United States person or a person located in the United States that is conducted under chapter 121 of such title, section 2709 of such title, or title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 (50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq.), and each such provision is superseded to the extent it authorizes such a search or access without a warrant described in section 3119(a)(1) of such title."

ops.w:
SEC. __. RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER LAW.
Section 3119 of title 18, United States Code, shall apply to any search of, or access to data pertaining to, a United States person or a person located in the United States that is conducted under chapter 121 of such title, section 2709 of such title, or title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 (50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq.), and each such provision is superseded to the extent it authorizes such a search or access without a warrant described in section 3119(a)(1) of such title.

am.cost: This change would name three laws and say the warrant rule overrides them. They are the Stored Communications Act, the FBI demand letter law and a foreign intelligence law. Any law not named would survive, so the list must be complete. This version leaves out bank reporting law and subpoenas issued without a court. Those would go on. The change would reshape how spy agencies collect data that affects Americans. It would also send the bill to more committees in Congress.

inq.q: Which laws let agencies get the kinds of data the surveillance bill covers without a full warrant from a judge?

items.h: A foreign spying law lets agencies collect data on foreign targets without a warrant for each one.
items.d: In 2022 this law on foreign spying covered nearly 250,000 targets. A court approved the program once a year, instead of a warrant for each target. That year the FBI ran roughly 119,000 searches of the collected data. The searches used details that identify Americans.

s.l: EPIC summary of the ODNI transparency report

items.h: The Stored Communications Act lets a judge order records handed over. It takes less proof than a warrant needs.
items.d: The Stored Communications Act lets a court order records turned over based on "specific and articulable facts". That means facts that can be clearly stated. That is a lower standard than the probable cause a warrant needs. Probable cause means good reason to believe a crime occurred.

items.h: The FBI can send letters to get customer records with no judge. They are called national security letters.
items.d: A federal law lets the FBI demand records about a company's customers and their dealings with it. The FBI only has to approve its own request. No judge takes part.

items.h: Banks must tell the Treasury Department when they see suspicious activity. No warrant is needed.
items.d: A federal law makes banks report suspicious activity to the Treasury Department. So the government gets money data about named people with no warrant. It does not even have to ask.

items.h: Many agencies can get business records with a subpoena, which is a legal order. No court is needed.
items.d: Dozens of laws let agencies demand business records with no court involved. Drug cases are one example.

items.h: Executive Order 12333, an order from the President, sets the rules for spying abroad.
items.d: Spying abroad is done under the President's power, not under a law passed by Congress. The surveillance bill changes federal criminal law. It does not mention Executive Order 12333.

inq.open: The legal references for these powers are listed so readers can check them. But the laws themselves were not opened for this review. The 2022 figures are the newest that were checked.

findings.pat: The party judges its own compliance
findings.title: Each agency would decide if collecting data needs a warrant. No one checks when the agency says no.
findings.plain: The bill would require a warrant, meaning permission from a judge, before the government searches a person's data. But the agency that wants the data would decide first if its own action counts as a search. It would also decide if one of the bill's exceptions applies, such as consent or an emergency. A judge would look at the matter only if the agency decided it needed a warrant. The bill requires no report or check when the agency decides it does not.
findings.tech: The warrant rule gives an outside check for searches that reach a judge. But the agency doing the investigating decides if a case ever reaches a judge. That agency gains from reading the word "search" narrowly and the bill's exceptions broadly. A person can sue only after learning about the search. The bill does not require anyone to tell them.
findings.use: An agency could decide that collecting someone's data needs no warrant under the surveillance bill. No judge, watchdog or member of the public would be told.

am.label: Yearly check of decisions not to seek a warrant
am.instr: Section 3119 of title 18, United States Code, as added by section 2 of this Act, is amended by adding at the end the following new subsection: "Audit.--The Inspector General of each agency that acquires data in reliance on an exception in subsection (b) shall audit a sample of those acquisitions each year and shall submit a report on the results to Congress, with a public summary.".

ops.w: Audit.--The Inspector General of each agency that acquires data in reliance on an exception in subsection (b) shall audit a sample of those acquisitions each year and shall submit a report on the results to Congress, with a public summary.

am.cost: This change would have each agency's Inspector General, its inside watchdog, check a sample of cases. These are cases where the agency collected data without a warrant. The checks would cost money. The public summary would need care so it does not reveal how investigations work. The President's branch of government picks these watchdogs. So their checks are less independent than a judge's review.

findings.title: The bill does not say when it would start or what happens to personal data agencies already hold.
findings.plain: The bill does not say when it would take effect. It also does not say what happens to data agencies already have.
findings.tech: With no start date, the bill would take effect as soon as it became law. It says nothing about keeping, deleting or still searching data gathered earlier. It also says nothing about investigations already under way.
findings.use: Agencies could keep using the sets of personal data they already hold.

findings.title: The bill does not require any reports or audits to show if agencies follow its new warrant rule.
findings.plain: The bill has no reporting rule and no audit, which is a formal check. It gives no role to an inspector general, the official who reviews an agency from inside. So there would be no regular way to know if agencies had stopped searching without warrants.
findings.tech: Surveillance laws often require yearly reports on court orders sought and granted. They also often require regular reviews by inspectors general. The right to sue depends on people learning they were searched. The bill does not require telling them.
findings.use: People could not challenge searches that break the bill's warrant rule if no one ever tells them about those searches.

findings.title: A sponsor says the bill stops federal pressure on local police to share data. The bill has no such rule.
findings.plain: One sponsor's press release says the bill would stop federal agencies from pushing local police to share surveillance data. No such rule appears in the bill as first filed.
findings.tech: The press release lists a ban on federal pressure on local police. The ban would cover data collected without a warrant. The bill says nothing about sharing data between governments or about rules tied to grants. It says nothing about fusion centers, which are shared federal and local intelligence offices. The ban may have been in an earlier draft.
findings.use: People who read the press release could think the bill already deals with federal pressure on local police. But the bill has no rule on sharing data.

s.l: Rep. Boebert press release

findings.title: The bill limits government access to data from companies that sell personal data. It does not stop the sales.
findings.plain: The bill tells the government not to get data from data brokers without a warrant. Data brokers are companies that sell personal data. A warrant is permission from a judge. The bill does not stop those companies from collecting or selling the data. The data would still exist. So any weak spot in the rule for government would leave the data open to it.
findings.tech: Past cases show why this matters. A Defense Intelligence Agency memo, made public in 2021, described buying location data from companies. A 2022 report, once secret and now public, described spy agencies buying data from companies on a large scale. In 2025 Montana barred its own agencies from buying such data. In 2024 the House passed a bill aimed at government purchases from brokers. Neither ends the collection itself.
findings.use: Any agency or partner the bill does not reach could still buy the data from data brokers.

am.label: Broader option: limit what data brokers may sell to governments
am.instr: Add at the end of the bill the following new section: "SEC. __. PROHIBITION ON PROVIDING COVERED DATA TO GOVERNMENT ENTITIES. (a) No data broker may sell, license, or otherwise provide data described in section 3119(d)(1)(C) of title 18, United States Code, to any Federal, State, local, or foreign government entity, or to any person acting on behalf of such an entity, except as required by a warrant. (b) A violation of this section shall be treated as an unfair or deceptive act or practice under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act."

ops.w:
SEC. __. PROHIBITION ON PROVIDING COVERED DATA TO GOVERNMENT ENTITIES.
(a) No data broker may sell, license, or otherwise provide data described in section 3119(d)(1)(C) of title 18, United States Code, to any Federal, State, local, or foreign government entity, or to any person acting on behalf of such an entity, except as required by a warrant.
(b) A violation of this section shall be treated as an unfair or deceptive act or practice under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act.

am.cost: This change would bar data brokers from selling personal data to any government body without a warrant. The Federal Trade Commission, which enforces rules on businesses, would enforce it. This goes beyond the bill's stated purpose. Limits on selling information face free speech challenges. The bill would need to define "data broker". And companies that collect data directly are not brokers. Banning data brokers altogether would go further. It would have larger effects on the economy and leave the same gap for companies that collect data themselves.
